Your fleet, in someone else’s field.

An agricultural contractor’s machinery is its advert. Drilling, spraying, baling, hedge cutting, muck spreading, drainage or harvest work puts your tractors, trailers and support vehicles in front of farmers and landowners across a wide area, and much of it is seen from the road. A consistent name and number across the fleet helps people remember who did the job, and who to ring next season.

Contractor fleets are mixed. A typical line-up might include tractors of different makes, grain or silage trailers, a low-loader, service vans and pickups for the operators. The livery has to work on all of them: the same name, colours and lettering style, scaled to suit each vehicle.

Big kit also means surfaces that don’t behave like van panels: curved bonnets, ribbed trailer sides, fibreglass cab roofs and painted steel that has seen years of weather. We look at each vehicle type and recommend where graphics will hold and where they will be seen.

What goes where.

Layout

Read from the road. Read across a field.

Machinery is usually seen from further away than a van, so lettering needs to be bigger and simpler. A trailer side or tank is the largest panel you own; a tractor bonnet is seen side-on from the lane; the back of a trailer is what queuing traffic reads.

Tractor bonnet or cabBusiness name
Trailer sides or tankName, service line and phone number, large
Trailer rearPhone number or web address, clear of lights, plates and reflectors
Vans and pickupsMatching name and contact details

Keep graphics clear of manufacturers’ safety labels, data plates and any reflectors or markings you are required to show. Where a panel is dented or ribbed, a fixed sign panel can sometimes work better than vinyl straight onto the bodywork.

From lettering to a fleet livery.

For vans and pickups, our published supply-and-fit packages, fitted within a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop, give a starting point. Tractors, trailers and machinery are quoted from photographs and sizes. All prices are “from” and + VAT, and your quote confirms them.

Practical points for contractors.

Timing around the season. Machinery is hardest to spare when it earns most. Plan graphics for quieter months and tell us your window when you enquire.

Fitting big kit. Vans and pickups come to our Norwich workshop. For tractors and trailers, tell us where the machine is kept and whether it can travel, and ask for a quote for on-site fitting if it can’t.

Surface condition. Weathered paint, rust and old decals need attention first. Vinyl follows the surface, so rough or flaking areas will show.

Lights, reflectors and markings. Trailers and machinery used on the road may need specific lights, reflectors or conspicuity markings. Check the current rules for each vehicle; we plan graphics around them, not over them.

Cleaning. Keep the pressure washer back from graphic edges and avoid strong solvents on vinyl.

What to send us.

For a contractor fleet quote, send:

  • A list of machines and vehicles: type, make, model and year.
  • Photographs of each side and the rear, with rough sizes of the main panels.
  • Your logo and colours, or an existing vehicle you want the rest to match.
  • The wording: business name, services, phone number and web address.
  • Where each machine is kept and whether it can come to Norwich.
  • Your quiet period, and any machines that must be done first.

Your questions. Answered.

Can graphics go on tractor bonnets?

Usually, on smooth painted areas. Heavily curved or vented areas, and panels that get hot, need more care. Send photographs and we will recommend positions.

Will vinyl stick to a ribbed or dented trailer?

Vinyl follows the surface, so ribs and dents show, and lettering that spans them can lift. We plan lettering to fit flat sections, or suggest a fixed sign panel.

Can you come to our yard?

Vans and pickups are fitted at our Norwich workshop. For machinery that can’t easily travel, ask for a quote for on-site fitting and we will confirm what is possible.

How much does contractor livery cost?

For vans and pickups, supply-and-fit packages start from £149 + VAT, within 30 miles of our Norwich workshop. Tractors, trailers and machinery are quoted from photographs and sizes.

How long will graphics last outdoors?

Using 3M and Metamark materials, our van graphics will last up to 7 years if looked after correctly. Machinery that is stored outside or pressure washed hard may need more attention.

Built for lanes, yards and field gates.

Rural vehicles are seen by fewer people than a city van, but by the right ones: neighbouring farms, estate managers, customers at the farm shop and everyone stuck behind you on a single-track lane. In a close-knit area, a recognisable name on a pickup or a horsebox builds a reputation across a whole district.

The conditions are tougher than on most business vehicles. Hedges brush the sides, mud cakes the lower panels, and vehicles are pressure washed after field work. Many are not vans at all: pickups with canopies, 4x4s, horseboxes, tractors and trailers all have curves, ribs and fittings that change where graphics can go. We keep key branding high, away from the dirtiest panels, and choose film to suit the surface.

Practical points for rural vehicles.

Keep it high. The bottom third of a farm vehicle is often hidden by mud. Put the name and number on the upper panels, canopy sides and tailgate.

Wash gently near the edges. Pressure washers are part of farm life. Keeping the lance back from graphic edges typically helps vinyl last much longer.

Roadside work. Tree surgeons and contractors working on or beside the highway may need reflective markings. Check the current guidance and your client’s requirements; see our Chapter 8 guide.

Machinery surfaces. Tractor and implement panels are often curved, ribbed or textured. Send close photographs of the area you want branded so we can check it is suitable.

Shows and sales. Horseboxes and show vehicles are judged on looks as well as identity. A clean, well-planned design on a horsebox can be refreshed between seasons without stripping the whole vehicle.

Graphics for people who notice details.

Automotive customers look closely at vehicles. A bubble, a lifted edge or lettering that does not follow a swage line will be spotted by the people you most want to impress. The standard of the graphics on your own vehicles says something about the standard of your work.

The vehicles vary widely. A dealership may want temporary branding on demonstrators that can come off cleanly before sale. A garage needs courtesy cars that remind customers where they came from. A mobile mechanic or valeter runs a van that is a workshop on wheels. A recovery operator needs a truck that is clearly identified, day and night, without looking like an emergency vehicle.

We also work with motorsport teams, from race car sponsor graphics to matching support vehicles and trailers. See race car graphics for that side of the work, and liquid wrapping for spray-on finishes.

Practical points for the motor trade.

Removal before sale. Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent. On sound factory paint, quality vinyl usually comes away cleanly, which suits demonstrators and courtesy cars that will be sold on. Tell us about any resprayed panels.

Manufacturer brand rules. Franchised dealers usually work to the manufacturer’s identity guidelines. Send them with your brief and confirm who signs off the artwork.

Recovery markings. Check the current rules and your insurer’s or client’s requirements for recovery vehicles and beacons. Do not copy emergency-service livery: battenburg-style and similar patterns are restricted, and we will not reproduce them.

Night work. Recovery operators and mobile mechanics often work after dark. Lettering can be cut in reflective vinyl so the name and number are visible in headlights.

Courtesy cars in rotation. Courtesy and loan cars change often. A simple, repeatable door and rear-window layout makes it quick to brand a replacement car and remove graphics from the one being sold.

No. Battenburg-style and other emergency-service patterns are restricted, and we will not copy them. Check the current rules and your client’s requirements for recovery markings, and we will design branding that stays clearly your own.

Breweries · distilleries · wine merchants · drinks wholesalers

Brewery & drinks delivery graphics.

Your delivery van visits pubs, shops and doorsteps every day. Graphics that carry the label design onto the road and tell the trade how to order.

DISCUSS YOUR DELIVERY VEHICLES ↗CALL 01603 407786

Norwich workshop · NR6 6AQ · Monday–Friday, 8:30am–5pm

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Food & drink / Brewery & drinks delivery graphics
What it needs to sayWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your vehicles ↗

Your label. On the road.

Drinks producers usually have strong branding already: a bottle label, a pump clip, a logo on the taproom wall. Delivery vehicles are where that identity meets two different audiences. Licensees and shop buyers see your van on the drop and want to know how to order. Drinkers see it in town and recognise the brand they had at the weekend.

Good drinks delivery graphics borrow from your labels without trying to reproduce every detail. Label artwork is designed to be read at arm’s length; a van is read from across the road. We pick out the elements that scale up, such as the logo, a key colour and an illustration, and add a clear line for trade orders.

Typical vehicles. Panel vans for local drops and taproom collections, Luton and box vans with tail lifts for casks and kegs, refrigerated vans for wine and soft drinks, and small electric vans for city deliveries. Larger operators may run several types, so the livery has to work across them.

What goes where.

Layout

Brand on the box. Orders on the doors.

On a box or Luton van, the box sides are large, flat and above the traffic, which makes them ideal for a big logo and brand illustration. The cab doors suit a smaller logo with the trade order line. The rear is read by drivers behind you and by staff at the cellar door.

Box sidesLogo, brand artwork and a short strapline
Cab doorsName and trade orders phone or email
Rear / shutter areaWeb address and shop or taproom details
Front / cab topName, readable in mirrors

Tail lifts, roller shutters, step plates and rear lights interrupt the rear. Photograph them in the open and closed positions so we can keep lettering on the panels that stay put.

From basic lettering to a full livery.

Many producers start with the logo and contact details, then move to printed livery as the fleet grows. Our published supply-and-fit packages apply to vans fitted within a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop. Prices are “from” and + VAT and confirmed by quote; box and Luton bodies are quoted individually.

Basic graphics, from £149 + VAT ↗

Single-colour cut vinyl name on the bonnet, both sides and rear, with phone and web address lower down.

Standard graphics, from £210 + VAT ↗

Adds social media details, a second colour or infill, and a cut or printed logo (subject to complexity and hi-res files).

Pro graphics, from £455 + VAT ↗

Up to three design ideas beyond the regular layout, and a large logo or graphic on the rear quarters and rear.

Printed livery & wraps ↗

Label-style artwork printed across the body or box. Quoted per vehicle, with consistent colours across a fleet.

Running several vehicles? Our fleet graphics page covers rollouts and keeping livery consistent. For budgets, read how much van graphics cost.

Practical points for drinks delivery.

Advertising codes. A liveried vehicle advertises your products. If it promotes alcohol, check your design against the current UK advertising codes on responsible alcohol marketing, and keep imagery and straplines sensible. We can adjust a design, but compliance decisions are yours.

Discreet or bold? Some businesses prefer not to advertise exactly what is in the back of a parked van. You can lead with the brand and keep product descriptions low-key; it is worth discussing with your insurer.

Matching your labels. Printed colours can differ slightly from your bottle or can print. Send your brand colour references and we will match as closely as the vinyl allows; cut lettering can use in-stock coloured vinyl.

Loading wear. Rear corners and areas around tail lifts take knocks from cages and kegs. We keep important graphics away from these zones, and individual panels can be replaced if they get damaged.

What to send us.

Bring the brand and the vehicles together with these details:

  • Make, model and body type of each vehicle, and how many there are.
  • Photographs of every side, with tail lifts and shutters open and closed.
  • Your logo and label artwork as vector or high-resolution files.
  • Brand colour references from your printer or brand guidelines.
  • Trade order phone and email, web address, shop or taproom details.
  • Which vehicles are leased, and any lease conditions on graphics.

You see the livery laid out on each body type, so a panel van and a Luton look like part of the same family.

Van packages start from £149 + VAT (Basic), £210 + VAT (Standard) and £455 + VAT (Pro) for vans fitted within 30 miles of our Norwich workshop. Box and Luton bodies and printed livery are quoted individually; the final price is confirmed by quote.

Yes, if you send the original files. We usually simplify it for the vehicle, because detail designed for a bottle can disappear at road distance.

Can we change the graphics when we launch a new beer?

Yes. Graphics are semi-permanent, so a seasonal panel can be replaced without redoing the whole vehicle. Keeping the core brand separate from promotional panels makes this simpler.

Our vans are leased. Is that a problem?

Usually not, but check your agreement first. Our graphics can be removed, and our guide to graphics on leased vans explains what to ask.

A van that works as a site board.

Builders and roofers get more from a parked van than almost any other trade. An extension, loft conversion or re-roof keeps you at one address for weeks, and the neighbours walk past your vehicles every day. Many of the next jobs come from exactly those people.

Those customers want to know three things. Do you do the kind of work they need? Are you an established firm they can trust with a large sum of money? How do they get in touch? Your name, a short description such as “Extensions · Renovations · New builds” or “Pitched & flat roofing”, and a clear number and website answer all three.

Architects, surveyors and main contractors see your vehicles on site too. A consistent look across the van, pickup and site boards tells them you run an organised operation.

Vans, pickups and tippers.

Crew-cab vansTransit or Sprinter crew cabs carrying a team and its kit

Branded stock. Sold with a clean finish.

A dealership’s vehicles do more advertising than most businesses’, but they are also stock. Demonstrators and promotional cars are driven, photographed and eventually sold, so the graphics need to look sharp for a season and then come away without marking paint that a buyer will inspect closely.

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Food & drink / Catering trailer graphics
What it needs to sayWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your trailer ↗

Flat panels. Long days on the pitch.

Unlike a food van, a catering trailer does almost all of its selling while unhitched. It sits on a pitch for a whole show weekend, a market day or a wedding reception, often side by side with a dozen other traders. The graphics are judged from the far end of the row, then again at the counter, by people deciding where to spend their money.

The good news is that trailers usually have large, flat, square panels, which are ideal for bold lettering and full-colour print. The temptation is to fill them. The most effective trailer layouts say what you sell in a few huge words high up, show one strong image, and keep everything else for the counter and menu board.

Typical vehicles. Purpose-built catering trailers with a side hatch, converted horseboxes serving drinks or pizza, compact kiosk trailers and box trailers used for storage at events. We also brand the towing vehicle so the pair match on the road; ask about it in the same quote.

What goes where.

Layout

Big words high. Menu at the counter.

Most catering trailers serve from one long side. When the hatch lifts, the panel above it becomes your most valuable space: it is visible over the heads of a queue. The panels either side of the hatch suit images and a short menu. The A-frame end and rear are seen while towing and from the walkways, so they suit booking details.

Above the hatchWhat you sell, in a few large words
Either side of the hatchProduct image and short menu
Front & rearName, web address and “book us for events”
Back sideName and logo for the next row of stalls

Measure the hatch, the counter and the open awning, and mark lockers, vents and electrical hook-ups. We keep critical lettering out of those areas so nothing is hidden when you are set up.

From lettering to a full colour wrap.

Our published van packages are a guide to what simple lettering costs on a vehicle, but trailers vary so much in size and construction that we quote them individually. Every price is “from” and + VAT, and confirmed by quote.

Lettering for the towing van, from £149 + VAT ↗

Our Basic van package covers single-colour cut vinyl name and contact details on a van fitted within 30 miles of Norwich.

Cut and printed trailer graphics ↗

Name, menu headings and contact details in cut vinyl, with printed panels where you want images. Quoted per trailer.

Printed part & full wraps ↗

Full-colour print across the trailer for a colour change or a photographic design, printed up to roughly 1.5m wide in-house.

Liquid wrapping ↗

A spray-applied alternative for changing the base colour of suitable bodywork. Ask whether it suits your trailer.

Need the towing vehicle done too? See van graphics or car graphics, and read cast vs calendered vinyl for why material choice matters on riveted panels.

Practical points for catering trailers.

Rivets, seams and corners. Many trailers are built from riveted aluminium or GRP panels. Vinyl has to be worked around rivet heads and over seams, which affects the film we choose and how a design is split. Close-up photographs help us plan this.

Parked outdoors all winter. A trailer that sits in a yard between seasons gets weathered on one side more than the other. Covering it, or parking it out of direct sun, typically helps graphics last longer.

Gas, power and ventilation. Do not cover vents, flues or labels your gas or electrical engineer needs to see. Check their requirements, and anything your council or event organiser asks for, before approving the design.

Plates and lights. Leave the number plate, lights and reflectors clear. We design the rear around them rather than over them.

What to send us.

Trailers are all different, so details matter more than usual:

  • Manufacturer and model of the trailer, or a description of the conversion.
  • Overall length and height, and measurements of each panel if you can.
  • Photographs of every side, closed and set up for service with the awning out.
  • Close-ups of rivets, seams, lockers and vents.
  • Your logo files, menu headings and the line that says what you sell.
  • Whether the towing vehicle should match.

01

Send your measurements and photos. If you are local, bring the trailer to the workshop and we can look at it together.

02

Approve a mock-up.

We set the design on your trailer’s panels, showing how it looks with the hatch open and closed.

03

Print and cut.

Your trailer is fitted at our Norwich workshop on a date agreed in advance of your first event.

Can you wrap an old horsebox conversion?

Often, yes. The condition of the bodywork matters most: flaking paint, filler and corrosion tend to show through vinyl, so tell us about any repairs when you send photos.

Should my menu be part of the wrap?

Usually not. Prices and dishes change, so we suggest separate menu boards or a replaceable panel, keeping the wrap for the parts of your brand that stay the same.

Can you match my towing vehicle?

Yes. We can design the trailer and the towing car or van together so they look like a set on the road, and quote both at once.

Charity & community vehicle graphics.

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Health, care & public sector / Charity & community vehicle graphics
What charities needWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your vehicle ↗

More than a logo on a door.

Charity and community vehicles cover a wide range: community transport minibuses, food bank and furniture reuse vans, youth and outreach buses, search and rescue support vehicles, charity shop collection vans and the one car a small charity uses for everything. People want to know who you are and how to help.

That usually means three messages competing for space: the charity’s name and purpose, a call to action (donate, volunteer, book a journey, request a collection), and the funders or sponsors who paid for the vehicle. Give the first two priority. Funder logos matter, but a side panel crowded with them is hard to read and can make the charity itself disappear.

Budgets are often tight and vehicles are kept for a long time, so think about what will date. A web address and a general phone number last longer than a named contact or a campaign slogan. Anything likely to change, such as a sponsor whose agreement ends, is best kept on its own panel.

What goes where.

Layout

Cause first. Thanks second.

People give a charity vehicle a little more attention than a trade van, especially when it is parked at an event or outside a shop. Use the sides to explain the cause in a few words and the rear to ask for something specific.

Bonnet & upper sidesCharity name and logo
SidesWhat you do, in one line, plus your registered charity number
Rear doorsDonate, volunteer or book, with your web address
Rear quarters or lower rearFunder and sponsor logos, grouped together

Check your funding agreement: some funders ask for their logo to appear at a particular size or position, and supply their own artwork. Tell us at the start so the layout works for everyone.

From simple lettering to a full livery.

Our published supply-and-fit van packages, for vehicles fitted within a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop, suit most charity vans. Minibuses, buses and trailers are quoted individually. Prices are “from” and + VAT, confirmed by quote.

Single-colour cut vinyl name on the bonnet, sides and rear, plus web address and phone number. A strong start on a small budget.

Standard graphics, from £210 + VAT ↗

Adds a logo, a second colour or panel infill and social media details, subject to complexity and hi-res files.

Pro graphics, from £455 + VAT ↗

Up to three design ideas and larger graphics on the rear quarters and rear, which gives funder logos room to breathe.

Photographic or full-colour designs that tell the story of your work. Quoted per vehicle.

If volunteers are happy to fit simple lettering themselves, supply-only kits are available from our online shop, from £95 + VAT for a Basic small van.

Practical points for charities and community groups.

Rescue and emergency styles. If your charity supports the emergency services or works in search and rescue, follow the livery standard your organisation or partner service sets and confirm what you are entitled to display. Battenburg chequers and other emergency-service markings are restricted; we won’t reproduce them without that entitlement, and we won’t copy police or ambulance livery.

Charity details. Many charities show their registered charity number on vehicles. Check your charity regulator’s current guidance on where the number must appear, and keep it legible.

Donated and second-hand vehicles. Old signwriting may need removing first, and faded paint can show a shadow where previous graphics were. Send clear photographs so we can advise.

Accessible vehicles. On community minibuses, keep graphics clear of ramps, lifts, grab handles and any emergency exit or safety labels.

Volunteer drivers. A contact number on the rear gives other road users a way to report a problem or say thank you, so make sure it reaches someone who answers.

What to send us.

To quote for a charity or community vehicle, send:

  • The make, model, year and colour, and whether the vehicle is owned, leased or on loan.
  • Photographs of both sides, the front and the rear, including any old graphics.
  • Your logo and any brand guidelines, plus your registered charity number if you have one.
  • Funder or sponsor logos in official artwork, with any placement rules they have given you.
  • The call to action: donate, volunteer, book a journey or request a collection.
  • Your budget and timing, especially if a grant has to be spent by a set date.

SEND YOUR VEHICLE DETAILS ↗

Share the story.

Tell us what the charity does, who funded the vehicle and what you want people to do when they see it.

Balance the layout.

Group them in one area, usually the rear quarters or lower rear, at a consistent height. Check each funder’s rules first; some specify a minimum size or a position.

Yes. Vinyl is semi-permanent, so a sponsor panel can be removed or replaced without redoing the whole vehicle.

Graphics that build trust.

Cleaning and property maintenance businesses sell trust before anything else. Domestic clients hand over keys and leave you alone in their home. Letting agents and landlords rely on you to turn a property round between tenants. Offices and facilities managers want a team that arrives in identifiable vehicles. The graphics should look professional, consistent and calm.

Customers in this sector compare a lot of similar firms, so clarity helps. “Domestic & office cleaning”, “End-of-tenancy cleans” or “Property maintenance & repairs” tells a reader where you fit. If you serve landlords and agents, say so; they are repeat customers worth attracting.

Many of these businesses run several smaller vehicles rather than one big van, and consistency matters more than size. When two or three liveried cars pull up at an office together, the client sees one organised company rather than a group of individuals.

Hand wash with mild soapy water and rinse. Avoid strong solvents and aggressive pressure washing at the edges. Looked after correctly, our van graphics will last up to 7 years.

Booked by groups who saw you at the gate.

Coaches and minibuses are booked by groups: schools arranging trips, sports clubs heading to away fixtures, wedding parties, care homes, social clubs and companies moving staff. The people who make those bookings often see your vehicles first at a school gate, a stadium car park, an airport drop-off or outside a venue. The livery is how they remember who you are, and how passengers find the right vehicle among several in a busy car park.

That gives coach and minibus graphics a slightly different brief from a trade van. The operator name and logo need to be bold and recognisable from a distance, and the overall look should feel clean, safe and well maintained, because parents and group organisers are choosing who to trust with people. A web address is usually more useful than a long list of services, with a phone number for quick quotes.

Typical vehicles range from van-based 16-seat minibuses and accessible minibuses with tail lifts, through midi coaches, to full-size touring coaches. Community transport groups and charities also run minibuses that need clear, friendly identification.

What goes where.

Layout

Work with the windows, not against them.

Much of a coach or minibus side is glass, so the solid panels below the windows and at the rear carry most of the graphics. Large brand shapes can sweep along the lower body and up the rear corners.

Lower sidesOperator name, logo and web address
RearName, phone number and web address, clear of lights and plates
FrontName or logo, kept clear of the windscreen
Near the doorFleet number for passengers and depot staff

Keep anything required on the vehicle, such as emergency exit markings and other signs, visible inside and out. We design around them from the start.

Rules and practical points.

Check before you cover glass. Passenger windows, emergency exits and the driver’s view are all areas where rules may apply. Perforated window film is often used on vehicle glazing, but whether it is acceptable on a particular window depends on the vehicle and its use. Check the current rules and your licensing requirements before planning any window graphics.

Licensing and contracts. Operators should check with their licensing authority, and with any client such as a council or school, whether specific markings, wording or signs are required. School transport has its own considerations; see our school minibus page.

Working under a client’s brand. If you run vehicles on contract for another operator, follow their livery standard and get approval before production.

Nothing that looks official. Avoid designs that could be mistaken for emergency-service livery. Battenburg-style patterns and similar markings are restricted, so do not copy them.

What construction vehicles need from their graphics.

Construction vehicles are seen in two places: on the road between yard and site, and on the site itself. On the road, the job is the same as any business vehicle: a clear name, a number and a recognisable look. On site, graphics also help people identify the contractor, the fleet number and which vehicle belongs to whom, and they may sit beside reflective markings your client or the work requires.

The vehicles are harder on graphics than a typical van. Tipper bodies are scraped by loads, skip lorries carry chains and hooks, scaffold wagons are loaded with tubes and boards, and everything is pressure washed. We position branding on the panels that survive the work, such as cab doors, headboards and body sides above the worst of the damage, and use materials suited to the surface.

Many firms in this group also run vans and pickups. A consistent layout across the lot, from the 3.5-tonne tipper to the site manager’s pickup, makes a small fleet look organised. For vehicles working on or beside the highway, see our highways & utilities page and the Chapter 8 guide.

What public fleets needWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your fleet ↗

Accountable on every street.

Public sector vehicles are paid for by the public and seen by them every day: refuse and recycling vehicles, highway tippers and gritters, housing repair vans, parks and grounds vehicles, pool cars and electric vehicles, library and outreach vans. Clear identification tells residents who is working in their street and gives them a way to ask a question or raise a concern.

Consistency is the main design task. One corporate livery has to work on a small electric car, a panel van, a tipper and a large truck, often bought at different times from different suppliers. A short set of rules covering logo position, colours, lettering style and fleet number placement makes every vehicle recognisable and makes new vehicles straightforward to match.

Public bodies also have procurement processes, brand teams and, sometimes, partners whose names must appear. Building those into the brief at the start saves rework: who approves the artwork, which purchasing route you need, and whether vehicles carry shared or partner branding.

What goes where.

Layout

One livery. Every vehicle type.

Fleet livery works best as a system rather than a single drawing. We set out where each element sits on each vehicle type, so a van arriving next year can be done to match without starting again.

Front doorsOrganisation crest or logo
SidesService name, e.g. “Highways” or “Housing repairs”
RearContact number or web address
Front and rearFleet number, in a consistent size and position

Highway and roadside vehicles may also need rear chevrons and reflective markings. Our guide to Chapter 8 chevrons explains the basics; check the current guidance and your highway authority’s requirements for each vehicle.

For individual cars and vans, our published supply-and-fit packages, fitted within a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop, give a guide. Fleet programmes, trucks and specialist vehicles are quoted on the full schedule. Prices are “from” and + VAT and confirmed by quote.

Practical points for public fleets.

Nothing that looks like the police. Enforcement, warden and patrol vehicles need to be identifiable, but they must not look like police or emergency vehicles. Battenburg chequers and similar emergency-service markings are restricted, and we won’t copy them. Check the current guidance, and your own legal advice, on the wording and markings your enforcement vehicles may carry.

Crests and brand guidelines. Send the corporate identity guidelines and master artwork from your communications team. Coats of arms often need redrawing for vinyl, and any redraw comes back to you for approval.

Changes of use and disposal. Vehicles move between services and are eventually sold. Semi-permanent vinyl can be removed or replaced, so a van can be re-branded for another department or cleared before sale.

Leased fleets. Check lease conditions on graphics and return condition; our guide to graphics on leased vans covers the questions to ask.

Downtime. Courtesy vehicles are available while a vehicle is off the road; ask about them when planning a rollout.

  • Any reflective or Chapter 8 requirements from your highway authority or client.
  • Procurement details: quotation and purchase order requirements, and who approves artwork.

We offer Chapter 8 reflective kits for most mainstream vehicles and can cut bespoke reflectives in-house. Check the current guidance and your highway authority’s requirements for each vehicle before ordering.

Can enforcement vehicles use high-visibility chequers?

Battenburg and similar emergency-service markings are restricted, and we won’t reproduce them for non-emergency vehicles. Take advice on what your enforcement vehicles may display, and we will design clear, identifiable graphics within that.

Do you work with purchase orders?

Yes. Tell us what your process needs, for example a formal quotation or a purchase order before work starts, and we will work to it.

Can old branding be removed before a vehicle is sold?

Yes. Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent and designed to be removed. The condition of the paint affects how cleanly they come off, so send photographs.

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Logistics & transport / Courier & delivery van graphics
What the van must sayWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your vans ↗

Two audiences on every drop.

A delivery van is seen by more people in a day than almost any other business vehicle: at the kerb on every street of the route, in loading bays, at business parks and in queues on the ring road. Courier graphics have two audiences. The person receiving the parcel wants reassurance that the van at the door is legitimate. The business watching from the next unit might need a same-day run tomorrow, and wants to know who you are and how to book.

That means the message is less about listing services and more about trust and recall. A clear company name, a description such as “Same-day courier”, “Pallet & parcel delivery” or “Multi-drop & light haulage”, and a phone number and web address that can be taken in at a glance. A tidy, consistent look across every van also signals that parcels will be handled with care.

Typical vehicles are small and medium panel vans, long-wheelbase high-roof vans, Luton bodies for bulkier work and, increasingly, electric vans for town-centre routes. Many owner-drivers run a single van; larger operators replace vehicles regularly and need graphics that can be repeated quickly.

What goes where.

Layout

The rear doors work hardest.

On a delivery route, the van is followed far more often than it is passed. Drivers sit behind it at lights, in traffic and while it is parked on a drop. The rear doors therefore carry the booking message, while the sides carry the name for people on the pavement.

Rear doorsName, services line, large phone number and web address
SidesName, logo and a short service line
Bonnet & frontName, for mirrors and loading bays

The rear doors are opened dozens of times a day, so we keep lettering away from handles, hinges and the shut line, where hands and parcels cause the most wear.

From basic lettering to a fleet livery.

Single-colour cut vinyl name on the bonnet, sides and rear, with phone and web address on the lower sides and rear doors.

Standard graphics, from £210 + VAT ↗

Adds social media details, a second colour or panel infill, and a cut or printed logo (subject to complexity and hi-res files).

Pro & fleet, from £455 + VAT ↗

Part & full wraps ↗

Practical points for couriers.

Working for a network? If you deliver on behalf of a carrier or retailer, your contract may require their livery, limit your own branding or ask for approval first. Check it before you order, and send us their brand guidelines if their livery is needed.

Early starts and dark evenings. Much delivery work happens in poor light. Reflective vinyl, cut in-house, can be used for lettering or rear details to help the van stand out in headlights. Keep lights, plates and windows clear.

Leased and short-term vans. Many delivery vans are leased or hired. Our graphics are semi-permanent and can be removed, but check your agreement first. Our lease guide covers the questions to ask.

Working vehicles. Local reputation.

Farm vehicles are seen by a small but important audience: neighbours, other farmers, merchants, contractors and, if you sell direct, your customers. A clear farm name on the pickup or 4x4 is often enough for the working side of the business. Graphics really earn their keep with diversification: a farm shop, butchery, egg round, campsite, wedding barn, pick-your-own or livery yard all need customers, and a well-branded vehicle parked in a market town tells people you exist.

Farm vehicles also live harder lives than most. Mud, dust, diesel, hedge cutting, livestock and frequent pressure washing all affect how graphics wear. Placement matters as much as design: keep lettering away from the areas that take the most abuse, such as the sills behind the wheels and the corners of a pickup bed.

Many farms run a mix of old and new vehicles. Older paint, plastic panels and textured trims don’t all suit vinyl in the same way, so tell us what you have and we will say plainly where graphics will work best.

What goes where.

Layout

Name on the doors. Number on the back.

On a pickup, double-cab or 4x4, the front doors are the main space: flat, at eye level and visible in a yard or car park. The tailgate is read by drivers stuck behind you on a lane, so put a phone number or web address there if you sell to the public.

Front doorsFarm or business name and logo
Rear doors or rear wingsWhat you sell or offer, e.g. “Farm shop · Free-range eggs”
Tailgate or canopyWeb address or phone number

Hard-top canopies and vans give larger flat panels for a farm shop or produce brand. Keep graphics clear of tow hitches, lights and number plates, and remember that a roll cover or load liner can hide part of the side.

From a name on the door to a farm shop livery.

Practical points for farm vehicles.

Washing. Keep the pressure washer lance well back from graphic edges and avoid harsh degreasers on vinyl. A gentle hand wash once the worst of the mud is off helps graphics last.

Bring it in clean. Vinyl needs a clean, dry surface. Bring the vehicle in washed so the panels can be properly prepared before fitting.

Plastic and textured panels. Textured bumpers, arch extensions and some canopy materials don’t hold vinyl well. We place graphics on smooth painted panels where possible.

Security. Some farms prefer not to advertise their address or what equipment is kept there. A name, web address and phone number are usually enough.

Road use. If a vehicle or trailer needs reflective or conspicuity markings for road use, check the current rules for that vehicle type. We can cut reflective vinyl in-house once you know what is needed.

  • The wording: farm name, what you sell, web address, phone number and social media.
  • Any trailers or machinery you want to match, with photographs and rough sizes.
  • When the vehicle can be spared, around lambing, harvest and other busy periods.

As carefully arranged as the bouquet.

A florist’s van is judged on taste. It parks outside churches and wedding venues, appears in the background of guests’ photographs, and pulls up at homes on birthdays and anniversaries. People who see it are often the next customers: the guest planning their own wedding, or the neighbour who needs flowers next week.

Most florists want three things on the van: the shop name in the same lettering as the shopfront or website, a short line about what you do (“Weddings · events · funeral tributes”, or “Same-day local delivery”), and the place people actually find you, which is often Instagram as much as the phone number. A photograph of your own work can make the van, but only if the image is sharp enough to print large.

Funeral work needs a little thought. The same van may attend a wedding in the morning and a funeral director’s in the afternoon. A calm, elegant design works for both; loud offers and bright novelty graphics do not.

Typical vehicles.

Small vans are the norm: Berlingo, Partner, Kangoo, Caddy and Transit Connect, sometimes a high-roof version for tall arrangements and wedding arches. Flower farms and event florists may add a medium van or a small trailer for staging, buckets and urns.

What goes where.

Layout

Let the flowers breathe. Keep the name clear.

On a small van there is less space than people think, so we keep the name large and let any floral image work as a backdrop rather than competing with it. The sides are what guests and passers-by see; the rear doors are where a follower behind you has time to note your handle or web address.

SidesShop name, floral image or pattern, short services line
Rear doorsWeb address, Instagram handle and phone
BonnetShop name or monogram

If the van has rear-door windows, we keep lettering clear of them or discuss a suitable window material. On a sliding side door, we place the design so it lines up when the door is shut and nothing important falls across the handle.

Adds your logo, social media details and a second colour, which is often enough for a soft, branded look.

Pro graphics, from £455 + VAT ↗

Up to three design ideas, with a large logo or floral graphic on the rear quarters and rear.

Printed floral photography or pattern across part or all of the van, quoted for your vehicle and artwork.

Practical points for florists.

Photographs must be big enough. A picture that looks perfect on Instagram may be far too small to print across a van side. Send the original camera file, not a screenshot, and we will tell you honestly whether it will hold up.

Think about heat. Flowers dislike a hot load area. Dark finishes absorb more sunlight, so if the van sits in the sun, a light base colour with floral detail is worth considering.

Busy weeks. Avoid booking fitting just before Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day or a big wedding weekend. Plan ahead, and ask about courtesy vehicles while the van is with us.

Keep it clean. The van is in wedding photographs. Hand washing with a mild cleaner keeps printed graphics looking fresh; harsh chemicals and pressure-washing at edges shorten their life.

When your vehicle is your shopfront.

For most mobile food and drink businesses the vehicle does two jobs. On the road it is an advert. Once parked at a market, festival or business park it becomes the shop itself, and customers decide in a few seconds whether to queue. The graphics need to say what you sell, look appetising and make it obvious where to order.

That changes the layout. The serving side matters more than the driver’s side, the area around the hatch has to stay clear for menus and the counter, and the brand often needs to be visible above a queue of people. A delivery vehicle for a brewery or drinks wholesaler is different again: it works more like a trade van, with the brand and a route to order front and centre.

Food vehicles are also cleaned more than most, inside and out, and spend long hours parked in the sun. We plan finishes and edges around that routine. Our food van wraps page covers full wraps for trucks, trailers and coffee vans in more depth.

A loan car that brings work back.

A tidy name, phone number and “courtesy car” line turns each loan into a small advert.

The tone matters. A loan car covered in sales messages can feel pushy to the customer driving it. Most garages do best with a clean, consistent design: name and logo on the doors, the services you are known for (servicing, MOT, diagnostics, tyres) in a short line, and the phone number and web address where people read them at junctions.

Typical vehicles. Small hatchbacks and electric cars used as courtesy cars, a collection-and-delivery van, a recovery or breakdown vehicle for local call-outs, and sometimes the owner’s own car. Matching them builds recognition even with only two or three vehicles.

Read across a site, not a driveway.

Groundworks and plant graphics are read by a different audience from a typical trade van. The people who matter most are site managers, quantity surveyors and other contractors: the people deciding who gets the next package of drainage, foundations or muck-away. They see your excavator from the cabin window, your dumper crossing the haul road and your pickup parked by the welfare unit. What they need to pick up is simple: whose machine it is, and how to reach that company again.

For plant hire firms there is a second job. A hired machine can sit on someone else’s site for weeks, so the graphics carry the hire desk number and a fleet number that site staff can quote when they ring about a breakdown, an off-hire or a swap. Clear numbering saves calls going to the wrong depot and makes yard checks quicker.

Typical vehicles in this work include 360 and mini excavators, site dumpers, rollers, telehandlers, the pickups and crew vans that carry the gang, and the tippers and low-loaders that move it all between jobs. Each has very different surfaces, and few of them are as flat or as clean as a van side.

What goes where.

Layout

Big numbers. Short name. Clear of the warnings.

On machines, the best positions are the flattest, least-scuffed panels that face outwards when the machine is working: counterweights, engine covers, cab sides and boom or dipper sides on larger excavators. On support vehicles, the familiar van layout applies.

MachinesCompany name and fleet number, sized to read across the site
Hire plantHire line phone number and depot
Pickups & vansName, services line, phone and web address

Keep lettering away from steps, grab handles, hinges and anything that is regularly kicked, chained or scraped. A logo that survives the first month on a dumper is one that has been placed with the machine’s working life in mind.

From fleet numbers to full livery.

Most groundworks firms need two levels: simple, tough identification on the plant and fuller branding on the road-going vehicles. Never cover safety labels. Machines carry manufacturer warning decals, lifting and load charts, and other statutory or safety markings. Graphics must work around them, not over them. Send photographs that show where they are, and tell us if any need replacing.

Surfaces matter. Plant panels are often textured, heavily curved, painted in machine-specific finishes or already patched. Vinyl needs a clean, sound surface to bond to, so machines should arrive or be presented degreased and dry. Expect a shorter life on panels that are constantly scraped or pressure-washed at close range.

Getting machines to us. Vans and pickups can come to our Norwich workshop. Tracked plant usually cannot, so ask for a quote for on-site fitting at your yard, or order cut lettering to fit yourselves.

Working on the highway? Vehicles working on or beside the road may need rear chevrons and reflective markings. Check the current guidance and your client’s requirements; see our highways & utilities page.

  • Your numbering system, including how you want numbers to read (for example a prefix and digits).

Ask for a quote for on-site fitting with your machine list and location. Alternatively, we can post cut lettering and fleet numbers for your own team to apply.

Use a system your depot already understands, keep the number short, and make it the same size and position on every machine of a type. We can produce the full set in one run so each number matches.

Several of these vehicles are regulated, or work for clients who set strict brand and identification rules. School transport, patient transport and anything that might be mistaken for an emergency vehicle all need particular care. We design around the requirements your organisation, commissioner or licensing authority gives us, and we will not copy emergency-service livery: battenburg-style patterns and similar markings are restricted.

Discretion matters too. Some care providers prefer modest branding outside clients’ homes, while a fundraising charity wants to be seen as widely as possible. The trade pages below cover both ends of that scale.

A brand that travels the country.

A lorry covers more miles in a year than almost any other business vehicle, and much of that time is spent on main roads, at distribution centres and in customers’ yards. HGV graphics are rarely about generating phone calls from passers-by. They build recognition: customers and suppliers see your trucks at their gates, other hauliers notice how well kept the fleet looks, and the public connects the name with reliability.

For many operators there is another reader who matters just as much: the driver. Recruitment is a constant concern in haulage, and a clean, confident livery with a short careers line and web address can do quiet but useful work at every truck stop and depot. Own-account fleets, such as builders’ merchants or food producers, use their lorries to put their brand in front of the trade customers they deliver to.

Typical vehicles are 7.5- to 26-tonne rigids with box, curtainside or refrigerated bodies, tractor units, and curtainside, box and fridge trailers. Each has different surfaces, and the plan for a cab is very different from the plan for a curtain.

What goes where.

Layout

The cab identifies the operator and carries the fleet number. The body or trailer sides carry the big brand message. The rear is shared with markings that may be required, so it is planned around them.

Box & trailer sidesLarge logo, strapline, web address or careers line

Required markings come first. Larger goods vehicles and trailers may need reflective conspicuity markings, rear marker plates and other statutory plates and labels. Graphics are designed around them, never over them.

Curtains. Curtainside curtains flex, fold and are tensioned every day, which is very different from a rigid panel. Whether vinyl graphics are suitable depends on the curtain material and condition. Tell us if you want curtains branded and we will be honest about what we can offer for them.

Units and trailers swap. If trailers move between tractor units, or are hired in, decide which carries your brand. Removable graphics on hired trailers should be agreed with the hire company.

Windscreens and windows. Keep the driver’s field of view clear. Check the current rules before planning any graphic on a windscreen or cab glass.

Trust first. Then visibility.

A home care agency’s cars do a different job from a trade van. They pull up outside the homes of older and vulnerable people several times a day, watched by families, neighbours and potential carers as much as new clients. Good graphics make the visit look organised and accountable.

There is a balance to strike. Some clients and families are happy for a branded car to be seen outside; others would rather the visit was discreet, because a marked care car can signal that someone at the address needs support. Many agencies settle on a modest logo and phone number on the front doors rather than large panels.

Recruitment is the other audience. Finding carers is a constant job for many agencies, and a car parked outside the supermarket with “Now recruiting carers” and a web address can reach people who never look at job boards. Keep that line separate so it can be removed or changed when you are fully staffed.

What goes where.

Smart on the showground. Clear on the road.

Horseboxes and trailers get graphics for two quite different reasons. For many owners it is about appearance: a yard name, the horses’ names, a stripe or pattern that makes an older box look smart again, or colours for a competition team. For businesses, such as livery yards, instructors, equestrian transporters and anyone towing a box trailer to shows and events, it is about advertising to everyone parked nearby or following on the road.

Both start with the same question: what is the box or trailer made of? Aluminium, painted steel, GRP and plywood panels, with ribs, rivets, hinges and vents, all affect what vinyl will do. Flat, smooth sections take cut lettering and printed panels well. Heavily ribbed or riveted sides need a layout that works around them.

Horsebox cut vinyl patterns and horse trailer revamps are both part of our vehicle graphics work. Whether you want a name on the groom’s door or a full colour change, we can produce a mock-up on your vehicle so you see the result before anything is made.

What goes where.

Layout

Name, pattern, contact.

On a horsebox, the long sides carry the main design, while the jockey door, ramp and groom’s door break up the panel. On a trailer, the sides and front are the largest surfaces, and the rear is mostly ramp or doors.

SidesYard or business name, stripes or pattern
Groom’s door or cab doorsHorse or rider names, logo
Rear ramp or doorsWeb address or phone number, if advertising
Front of trailerName or logo, visible when parked

Keep graphics clear of lights, number plates, reflectors, vents and hinges. Lettering that crosses a ramp edge or hinge line will be cut there, so we plan breaks in the design to match.

Cut vinyl names & patterns ↗

Lettering, stripes and patterns cut from our stock of coloured vinyl. The simplest way to personalise a box.

Printed panels & logos ↗

Full-colour logos, sponsors or photographic panels, ideal for yards, teams and businesses.

Part & full wraps ↗

A colour change or printed design across the whole box or trailer, for a full revamp of tired paint.

Liquid wrapping ↗

A sprayed-on finish and an alternative to vinyl for some surfaces. Ask whether it suits your box.

Considering a full wrap on a box with complex curves? Read about cast and calendered vinyl, which behave differently over shapes.

Practical points for horseboxes and trailers.

Security. Think twice before putting the yard’s address or postcode on a box or trailer that is often left unattended. A name and a web address or phone number are usually enough.

Condition first. Oxidised aluminium, chalky paint, old decals and corrosion around rivets all need dealing with before graphics go on. Vinyl over a poor surface tends to lift or show every flaw.

Lights, plates and markings. Lights, number plates, reflectors and any markings you are required to carry must stay visible. Check the current rules for your vehicle type.

Colour changes. If a wrap changes the main colour of a registered horsebox, check the DVLA’s current guidance on whether you need to update the vehicle’s details.

Season dates. Many owners want the box ready for the first show of the season. Tell us your date when you enquire.

  • Whether you want cut lettering, printed panels, a part wrap or a full colour change.
  • Any old graphics that need removing.
  • The date you need it back, such as the first show of the season.

Yes. Names are usually cut from coloured vinyl in a lettering style that matches the rest of the box, and can be changed as horses come and go.

Can you wrap an old horsebox?

Often, yes. A wrap can give an older box a new colour, but the surface has to be sound: corrosion, flaking paint and failed sealant need repairing first. Send close-up photographs and we will advise.

Will vinyl stick to aluminium?

Vinyl generally adheres well to clean, sound aluminium and painted panels. Oxidised or chalky surfaces, rivet heads and seams need care, so we check photographs before recommending a method.

Every box and trailer is quoted from photographs and sizes, because shapes and materials vary so much. Names and stripes cost far less than a full wrap. Prices are + VAT and confirmed by quote.

Yes. Box trailers have large flat sides that make good mobile signs. Keep the message short: name, what you do and a web address or phone number.

Instantly recognisable. Street to seafront.

An ice cream van has two audiences at once. Children decide from a distance, mostly on colour, pictures and the sense that something fun has arrived. Parents decide up close, looking for prices, what you sell and whether the van looks clean and well run. Good graphics serve both without clutter.

From across a park or a promenade, bold colour and one or two big images of cones, lollies or a character do more than any wording. Your trading name should be large and simple, because it is what people search for when booking you for a wedding or school fair. A phone number and web address belong on the road side and rear, where people read them while you are driving or parked.

Rear warning panels. Many operators carry a rear panel reminding drivers to watch for children. If you want one, tell us the wording your council, insurer or trade association recommends and we will make it large and clear; we will not invent wording for you.

Only if you supply official artwork you are allowed to use, usually from your supplier. Otherwise our designers can draw original illustrations that are yours to keep.

Two kinds of garden customer.

Landscaping and garden work splits into two kinds of customer. There are one-off projects (a new patio, fencing, turf, a full redesign) where the homeowner is choosing between firms and wants to see you are capable. And there are regular rounds: mowing, hedges and seasonal tidy-ups, where people want someone reliable who already works nearby. Both groups notice who is working in their street.

Say clearly which side you are on. “Garden maintenance” and “Landscaping & design” attract different enquiries. If you do both, put the work you want more of first. A phone number readable from across the road matters more than a list of services, because people often spot your vehicle while you are working and look you up later.

Practical points for garden and landscaping vehicles.

Mud, sap and clippings. Garden vehicles work hard. Wash graphics by hand with a mild cleaner, rinse off tree sap and bird droppings promptly, and keep pressure-washer jets away from vinyl edges.

Tailgates take knocks. Tipper tailgates and dropsides are loaded, unloaded and scraped every day. We keep fine detail off the most worn areas and put the number where it is better protected.

Waste and registrations. If you carry green waste or other people’s waste, check the current rules on any registration you need and whether you want to display it. Supply the exact wording and we will add it neatly.

Seasonal changes. Vinyl is semi-permanent, so a seasonal line such as hedge cutting or fencing can be added or swapped later without redoing the design.

Vinyl copes with everyday wear, but sharp branches and loads dragged across a tailgate can mark any surface. We keep important details away from the worst-hit areas, and a damaged section can be replaced without redoing the vehicle.

Reassurance on the doorstep.

Most locksmith customers are not browsing. They are locked out on a doorstep, standing by a car with the keys inside, or dealing with a break-in. They have usually found you on their phone, and when a van pulls up they want instant reassurance that it is the business they rang. Your name, written exactly as it appears online, and a clear phone number do that.

Other work is planned: landlords changing locks between tenants, homeowners upgrading to insurance-approved locks, businesses adding access control or safes. Those customers notice your van locally and keep the number for later, so a short line such as “Lock changes · Lockouts · Security upgrades” earns its place. Auto locksmiths should say so plainly; car key work is a separate search for most people.

Locksmithing is about security, so the van should look solid and established. Strong, simple lettering in a confident colour suits the trade better than busy graphics.

Readable in the dark.

Lockouts happen at night and in the rain. Contrast matters more than style: light lettering on a dark van or dark lettering on a light one. Reflective vinyl can be used for the name or number so the van picks up headlights and torchlight; we cut bespoke reflectives in-house.

Match your online name. Customers compare the van with the listing they found. Use the same business name, logo and number as your website and online profiles so there is no doubt.

Graphics for vehicles that never stop moving.

Transport vehicles cover more ground than almost any other business vehicle, so the graphics are seen by more people. They also face more wear: high mileage, motorway grime, frequent washing and, for coaches and minibuses, constant passenger use. The design has to stay clear at speed and survive the routine.

Large vehicles offer large, flat panels. A Luton box or a lorry body can carry a bold brand, but size alone does not make it effective. Long lines of text are hard to read on a moving vehicle; a strong name, one line about the service and a web address usually work better than a full list of destinations.

Many operators in this group run more than one vehicle, and some carry passengers, so there are often rules to check about markings, operator details or licensing. Graphics should be planned to sit alongside whatever your licensing authority or client requires. Our fleet graphics and taxi & private hire pages cover two related cases.

What it needs to sayWhat goes whereOptions & pricesPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your van ↗

A small van. A big first impression.

Mobile coffee is a regulars’ business. Many vans work the same pitches each week: a station forecourt at 7am, a business park at lunchtime, a sports club on Saturday. The graphics need to be recognisable at a glance from a queue of traffic, and good enough that a commuter is happy to buy from a van they have never tried.

That usually means a confident name, a simple mark and a style that suggests the coffee you serve, whether that is speciality single-origin or quick and friendly. Too many words make a small van look cluttered. Save the menu, the loyalty offer and the “where we are this week” details for boards and a QR code near the serving point, where people stand and wait.

Typical vehicles. Coffee businesses often run compact vans such as the Volkswagen Caddy, Renault Kangoo or Citroën Berlingo with a rear-door bar, plus three-wheeled tuk-tuks, vintage-style vans and converted horseboxes. Small vehicles have small flat areas, so every panel has to earn its place.

What goes where.

Layout

Name on the sides. Menu where people queue.

On a compact van that serves from the rear doors, the doors become the shop counter once open, and the graphics on them disappear. Plan for both states: the name and a short description on the sides and bonnet for when the doors are open, and booking details on the outside of the doors for when you are on the move.

BonnetTrading name
Side panelsName, mark and “speciality coffee” style line
Rear doors (closed)Phone, web and social handles
Serving areaMenu board and QR code

If you serve from a side hatch instead, the serving side carries the main identity and the road side becomes the travelling advert. Tell us how you set up on a pitch and we will design around it.

From simple lettering to a full wrap.

Many coffee vans start with clean cut-vinyl lettering on a coloured base, then move to a printed wrap once the brand is established. Our published supply-and-fit packages are for vans fitted within a 30-mile radius of the Norwich workshop; prices are “from”, + VAT, and confirmed by quote.

Practical points for coffee vans.

Steam, milk and spills. Graphics near the serving point get splashed with milk and coffee and wiped many times a day. Keep fine detail away from the counter, and clean with a soft cloth and mild detergent rather than strong solvents.

Opening doors and awnings. Mark hinges, gas struts, awning brackets and any fold-out counter on your photos. We keep lettering clear of shut lines and handles so nothing is cut through or hidden when you open up.

Permissions are yours to check. Pitches, street trading consent and food hygiene registration sit with your local council and landowners. Graphics do not change any of that, so check before you print a regular location on the van.

Keep the van earning. If you also use the van for catering bookings, ask about our courtesy vehicles when you book, so you are not left without transport while the graphics are fitted.

Small vans are quick to quote when we have the right details:

  • Photographs of each side with the doors or hatch open and closed.

  • The wording you want: name, style line, social handles and booking contact.
  • Whether you serve from the rear doors, a side hatch or a counter.

It can be, because a small van has less surface to print. On the other hand, a strong base colour with well-placed cut lettering often looks just as smart. We can show you both on a mock-up.

Can I add a QR code?

Yes. Put it near the serving point where people stand still, at a size that scans comfortably, and link it to a page you can update rather than one that might change address.

Can the graphics come off when I sell the van?

Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent and designed to be removed. On sound original paint they usually come away cleanly; resprayed panels carry more risk.

A salon brand on four wheels.

Mobile hair and beauty businesses are built on recommendation, and the car parked outside a client’s home is the moment a neighbour asks, “Who does your hair?” The graphics should answer before anyone asks: your name, what you do, and where to book.

Clients in this sector book through Instagram, Facebook or an online booking link far more than by phone. Give the handle real prominence, and keep services to a few words: “Mobile hairdresser · cuts, colour & bridal” or “Nails · lashes · brows”. A clean logo in your salon colours does more for trust than a long list of treatments.

Restraint pays off on a car. A hatchback has far less flat panel than a van, and it is often also the family car. Many mobile stylists choose door lettering and a rear-window or boot-lid line, which look smart and keep the car pleasant to drive off duty.

Typical vehicles.

Mostly small hatchbacks and city cars, such as a Fiesta, Corsa, Polo, Fiat 500, Mini or a small electric car, plus some small SUVs. A few busier businesses, carrying a portable basin or treatment couch, move up to a small van such as a Caddy or Berlingo.

What goes where.

Layout

Doors for the name. Rear for the booking.

Front and rear doors give the biggest flat area on a car, so the name and logo go there, sized to sit between the wheel arches and clear of handles and mouldings. The rear is read by the driver behind you, so it carries the booking route: handle, website or a simple “Book online”.

A clinic people can find.

Mobile healthcare vehicles take services to people: screening and vaccination units, outreach vans for rural or hard-to-reach communities, mobile dental, hearing or eye services, health promotion stands, and pharmacy or medical delivery vans. Each one needs to say, quickly and calmly, what it is and who it is for.

That puts wording first. The service name should be readable from across a car park, followed by one plain line about what happens inside (“Free health checks”, “Hearing tests”, “Drop-in clinic”). Opening times and booking details change, so they are better on a removable panel or a sign by the door than built into the main livery.

Many of these vehicles are run by, or on behalf of, an NHS organisation, a council or a provider working under contract. That brings brand guidelines and approval steps. Ask your communications team or commissioner for the identity rules and approved artwork before design starts, and allow time for their sign-off.

What goes where.

Layout

Entrance side, eye levelWhat happens inside, who it is for, the way in

Many pest control firms handle this by keeping the main branding calm: a clear business name, a neutral line such as “Pest control & prevention” or “Environmental services”, and a phone number. Pictures of insects and rodents are left off or kept small. People who need you still recognise the trade; people who don’t won’t give the van a second look.

Should I put the Gas Safe logo on my van?

If you are registered, customers often look for it. Check the Gas Safe Register’s current guidance on displaying its logo and your registration number before ordering, and supply the official artwork. We place it where it is easy to read, usually on the rear doors and lower sides.

Can I show an emergency or 24-hour number?

Yes, if the line is genuinely answered at those times. A separate out-of-hours number can go on its own line, so it is easy to swap later.

I’ve started fitting heat pumps. Can you add that without redoing the van?

Usually, yes. Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent, so a service line can be removed and a new one fitted, leaving the rest of the layout in place. Bring the van in and we will check the space available.

Promotional vehicle graphics.

A vehicle that is the advert. Bold graphics and wraps for launches, campaigns and roadshows, made to be seen and, when the campaign ends, removed.

DISCUSS YOUR CAMPAIGN ↗CALL 01603 407786

Norwich workshop · NR6 6AQ · Monday–Friday, 8:30am–5pm

Vehicle graphics / Sectors / Events & leisure / Promotional vehicles
What people readWhat goes whereOptionsPractical pointsWhat to send usProcessFAQsDiscuss your campaign ↗

Built to stop people in their tracks.

Most vehicle graphics support a business that has another job to do. A promotional vehicle exists to be noticed: a car for a product launch, a van touring shows and town centres, a sampling vehicle at an event, or a striking wrap that makes the brand impossible to miss. That changes the brief completely.

The message should be one idea, not a brochure. A campaign line people can read in two seconds, a strong image, the brand, and one call to action, such as a short web address, a hashtag or a QR code for people standing nearby. Everything else is noise to someone driving past.

Promotional vehicles are also photographed and shared. Clean, high-impact design, accurate colours and tidy finishing at the edges matter more here than on almost any other vehicle, because the vehicle itself is the content.

Typical vehicles.

Small cars and city cars for launches and brand ambassadors, often a Mini, Fiat 500 or electric hatchback; panel vans and box vans for roadshows and sampling; pickups and 4x4s for outdoor brands; and trailers for exhibition stands and displays.

What goes where.

Layout

One message per side. One action at the back.

Each side should work alone, because most people only ever see one. The rear is where people stand or queue behind the vehicle, so it is the place for the call to action. Roofs can carry a logo where the vehicle will be seen from above, such as at an event or in a multi-storey car park.

SidesCampaign line, hero image and brand
RearWeb address, hashtag or QR code
Roof and bonnetLogo or campaign mark

We check every image against the vehicle’s panels, so that faces, products and text do not fall across door gaps, handles or wheel arches.

From campaign lettering to a full wrap.

Promotional work is quoted for your vehicle, coverage and campaign length. For simpler campaign lettering on a van, our supply-and-fit packages start from £149 + VAT (Basic), £210 + VAT (Standard) and £455 + VAT (Pro), within a 30-mile radius of Norwich. Prices are “from”, and your quote confirms the figure.

Campaign graphics ↗

Printed campaign line, logo and call to action on the sides and rear, for a shorter or lower-budget campaign.

Full printed wraps ↗

The whole vehicle becomes the advert, printed on our 8-colour, 1440dpi printers.

Part wraps ↗

Printed coverage of the rear half or lower panels, combined with the vehicle’s own paint colour.

Liquid wrapping ↗

A sprayed colour change, which can be combined with vinyl campaign graphics.

Need matching banners or display boards for the roadshow? Our signage team can produce them from the same artwork, and our design department can develop the campaign creative.

Practical points for promotional vehicles.

Plan the removal. Campaigns end. Our vehicle graphics are semi-permanent, so they can be removed, but on leased or hired vehicles check the agreement and the return-condition rules first.

Parked advertising. If the plan is to park the vehicle as a static advert, check with the local council and the landowner before you do. Rules on advertising vehicles vary.

Check your claims. Advertising on a vehicle is still advertising. Make sure prices, offers and claims are accurate and follow the advertising rules that apply to your sector.

Launch dates. Tell us the launch date at your first enquiry. Artwork approval drives the schedule, and we agree fitting dates rather than promising them.

What to send us.

Gather these before you get in touch:

  • Make, model and year of each vehicle, and whether it is owned, leased or hired.
  • Photographs of every side, taken square on.
  • Campaign artwork or brand guidelines, logos as vector files and images at full resolution.
  • The campaign line and call to action, including any QR code destination.
  • Campaign start and end dates, and where the vehicle will be used.
  • Whether the graphics must be removed at the end.

Can the graphics be removed after the campaign?

Yes. Vehicle graphics are semi-permanent and designed to be removed. On sound factory paint, quality vinyl usually comes away cleanly.

Can you work from our agency’s artwork?

Yes. Send the artwork and brand guidelines, and we adapt it to the vehicle’s panels and show you a mock-up before production.

Should we use a QR code?

On the rear, where people stand close, a QR code can work well. Make it large, test it, and link to a page that stays live for the whole campaign.
